summary: The work explores price cycles and regulatory settlement mechanics in GME trading, focusing on SLD cycles tied to monthly option expiration on the 3rd Friday of each month and T+ settlement cycles. The author claims IT expertise and describes DTCC/NSCC system operations, discussing how fails-to-deliver might be obscured through regulatory exemptions (ODS, X-REORG flags) and speculating that GameStop management could exploit system vulnerabilities to force short covering via corporate reorganizations. While referencing real DTCC mechanisms and regulatory terminology, the work provides minimal primary-source documentation and rests largely on interpretive inference and author-assigned confidence scores. Core predictions—that specific cycles would drive predictable price movements—did not materialize by 2026.

key_claims.claim: Claims that SLD (Supplementary Liquidity Deposit) cycles tied to monthly option expiration cause predictable price movements in GME
key_claims.note: Pages 3-9. Author assigns 9/10 confidence to SLD cycles. However, no consistent price patterns attributable to SLD cycles are evident in hindsight. The Jan 28, 2021 alignment is correlational; the SEC's October 2021 report attributed the Jan 2021 run-up to positive-sentiment buying, not settlement mechanics.

key_claims.claim: Claims that T+21 and T+35 calendar-day cycles used to drive GME price movements but no longer do so effectively
key_claims.note: Pages 10-12. Author explicitly acknowledges C+21 is 'mostly horse shit' with 3/10 confidence and C+35 barely moves GME. This honest self-correction aligns with hindsight: these cycles were hyped in SuperStonk but failed to produce consistent moves.

key_claims.claim: Claims that FTDs can be hidden through One Day Settling exemptions and Obligation Warehouse mechanisms where trades never pass through CNS
key_claims.note: Pages 14-15. Author includes explicit warning: 'not 100% verified.' While ODS exemptions exist in DTCC rules, the claim that obligations can be permanently excluded from CNS lacks primary-source documentation and remains speculative.

key_claims.claim: Claims that X-REORG flags allow obligations to be exempt from mandatory corporate reorganization events triggered by GameStop management
key_claims.note: Pages 15-17. X-REORG field exists in DTCC systems, but the claim that it allows obligations to escape reorganization-forced covering is unsourced inference. GameStop executed a 4-for-1 stock split in July 2022 with no forced covering, but this does not definitively test the mechanism.

key_claims.claim: Claims that RC (Ryan Cohen) is aware of DTCC vulnerabilities and will exploit them via corporate actions to force short covering
key_claims.note: Pages 17-18. Author speculates RC 'hopefully' knows about these mechanisms and will use them. No evidence presented that RC has or will act on any such knowledge. No forced liquidations materialized.

key_claims.claim: Claims that the DTCC operates legacy IT systems with exploitable vulnerabilities due to outdated technology and weak regulation
key_claims.note: Page 13. Author claims IT expertise but explicitly refuses to provide sources. DTCC's use of older systems is documented, but specific exploitable vulnerabilities are unsubstantiated.

key_claims.claim: Claims that the January 28, 2021 Robinhood margin call was triggered by or aligned with SLD cycle settlement mechanics
key_claims.note: Pages 7-9. Author correlates Jan 28 to the SLD cycle window. However, the SEC's October 2021 report concluded the Jan 2021 run-up was driven primarily by positive-sentiment buying, not settlement mechanics or margin calls.

key_claims.claim: Claims that overlapping multiple C+ cycles with SLD cycles now produces negligible price effects on GME
key_claims.note: Page 12. Author states even overlapped cycles barely move GME's price. This matches hindsight: predicted multiplier effects from overlapping cycles failed to materialize.

validity_rationale: The work mixes genuine regulatory information (SLD cycles, DTCC legacy systems, DTCC field codes like ODS and X-REORG) with largely unsubstantiated speculation about exploitable vulnerabilities and price causation. Against hindsight: predicted cycle-driven price movements failed to materialize; the SEC attributed Jan 2021 to sentiment, not mechanics; the July 2022 stock split triggered no forced covering; no systemic failures were exposed. The author shows some self-correction by honestly admitting T+ cycles no longer work and assigning them low confidence, which is more credible than broader SuperStonk claims. However, core predictions remain falsified and primary-source documentation is absent throughout. Rated 2/5 because speculation and unverified inference dominate, though explicit disclaimers and some honest acknowledgment of failed predictions mitigate worst framing seen elsewhere in the library.
topics: GME price prediction and trading cycles
